# Preface {.unnumbered}

Cells process information with networks of interacting proteins, genes, and
small molecules. To understand how these networks behave, we write down what
we know about their parts and interactions and ask what that knowledge
implies. Mathematical models make that question precise. This book teaches
**rule-based modeling**, an approach to building such models that suits
networks of proteins with many interaction sites, using the
[BioNetGen](https://bionetgen.org) language and tools
[@Blinov2004; @Faeder2009; @Harris2016].

## Who this book is for

The book has three audiences in mind:

- **Students** in courses on computational and systems biology. The early
  chapters assume a little calculus and some Python, but no prior modeling
  experience.
- **New members of a modeling lab** who need to become productive with
  rule-based models: building them, simulating them, fitting them to data, and
  sharing them.
- **Experimental and computational biologists** who want a practical
  introduction to the BioNetGen tools.

## How the book is organized

Each chapter introduces one set of ideas and applies them to a running
example, a cytokine signaling circuit in which STAT transcription factors
induce their own inhibitor, SOCS. The chapters are grouped into parts.

**Part I. Foundations**

- @sec-reaction-networks: Builds the
  STAT–SOCS circuit one reaction at a time and shows how a reaction network
  becomes a set of differential equations.
- @sec-rules: Shows why naming every complex
  by hand breaks down, and how rules that act on structured molecules solve
  the problem.
- @sec-stochastic: Describes reactions
  among small numbers of molecules with the chemical master equation and
  Gillespie's algorithm, and follows the noise from a single SOCS gene
  through the feedback loop.
- @sec-rules-guide: Writes rules for binding,
  enzymatic modification, synthesis and degradation, and aggregation, and
  checks each one against the reactions BioNetGen generates.

**Part II. Building realistic models**

- @sec-compartments: Places the circuit in a
  cell with a nucleus and endosomes, and shows how compartment sizes scale the
  rates of reactions.
- @sec-network-free: Simulates models whose
  networks are too large to generate, using receptor aggregation as the
  example.
- @sec-analysis: Computes conservation laws, steady
  states and their stability, dose–response curves, sensitivities, and
  bistability.
- @sec-energy-modeling: Assigns free energies to molecular structures so
  that cooperative binding satisfies detailed balance, and distinguishes
  equilibrium from signaling driven by ATP hydrolysis.

**In preparation.** Part III, *Models meet data*, will cover parameter
estimation, uncertainty and identifiability, building and sharing models, and AI-assisted modeling. Part IV
will cover advanced topics, including spatial simulation, rare events, and
visualization, and Part V will present case studies. The plan for the full
book is in
[`BOOK_PLAN.md`](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen-book/blob/main/BOOK_PLAN.md).

Every model in the book is in the
[`models/`](https://github.com/RuleWorld/bionetgen-book/tree/main/models)
folder of the book's repository, organized by chapter, and every figure is
produced by running those models. Each chapter ends with exercises. Lecture
slides and a printable worksheet for a course based on Chapters 1 and 2 are in
the [course repository](https://github.com/jrfaeder/RBM_Intro_BioNetGen).

## Tools

You can run the models in this book in three ways:

1. In a web browser, with no installation, using
   [BNG Playground](https://ruleworld.github.io/bngplayground/).
2. In Visual Studio Code with the BioNetGen extension, which provides
   syntax highlighting, one-click simulation, and plotting.
3. From Python, using [bngsim](https://bngsim.readthedocs.io) for fast ODE
   and stochastic simulation. This is how the figures in the book are made,
   it runs every model in the book, and it is the route to the analysis and
   fitting covered in later chapters.

@sec-installation explains how to install them, and @sec-bngl-reference
summarizes the syntax of BNGL.

## Conventions

BNGL code is shown in shaded blocks:

```bngl
begin reaction rules
  LRbind: L(r) + R(l) <-> L(r!1).R(l!1) kon, koff
end reaction rules
```

Python code that produces a figure is shown above the figure in the web
version of the book. Unless stated otherwise, concentrations are in
micromolar (µM) and time is in minutes. The parameter values in the running
example are illustrative, chosen to show the behavior clearly rather than
fitted to a particular cell type.

## Acknowledgments

BioNetGen began in the Cell Signaling Team at Los Alamos National
Laboratory, which Byron Goldstein founded. The team included his late wife,
Carla Wofsy, together with Tony Redondo, Bill Hlavacek, Michael Blinov, and
me. The problem that led to BioNetGen, the combinatorial complexity of the
complexes that form in receptor signaling, came out of that team's work
[@Hlavacek2003], and the first version of the software was written there
[@Blinov2004].

I thank Byron and the rest of the Cell Signaling Team at that time, Tony,
Carla, and Bill, for inviting me to join them in their odyssey to map and
model the world of biological complexes.

Many people have contributed to BioNetGen and the tools built around it
since then. Development moved to my group in the Department of
Computational and Systems Biology at the University of Pittsburgh, where
Leonard Harris, Justin Hogg, José-Juan Tapia, John Sekar, Sanjana Gupta,
Ilya Korsunsky, Arshi Arora, Dipak Barua, and Robert Sheehan contributed to
BioNetGen 2 [@Harris2016]. Leonard Harris and Justin Hogg led the
development of compartmental BNGL [@Harris2009]. John Sekar and Justin Hogg
led the development of energy-based modeling [@Sekar2016], and John Sekar
and José-Juan Tapia led the development of the automated visualization of
rule-based models used in @sec-rules [@Sekar2017Visualization]. José-Juan
Tapia also led the development of Atomizer, which converts reaction-network
models into rule-based models. Michael Sneddon led the development of NFsim,
in a collaboration with Thierry Emonet [@Sneddon2011]. Arvind Rasi
Subramaniam, now an investigator at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in
Seattle, pioneered the use of rule-based models to describe translation and
also contributed to NFsim. Wen Xu and Adam Smith led the development of
RuleBender, a graphical interface for BioNetGen, in a collaboration with
G. Elisabeta Marai [@Xu2011], and Yao Sun and Robert Clark also contributed
to it. Ali Sinan Saglam created PyBioNetGen and the BioNetGen extension for
Visual Studio Code, with contributions from Alex DiBiasi, Nika Zaslavsky,
Caleb Armstrong, and Achyudhan Kutuva. Nika Zaslavsky, a Carnegie Mellon
undergraduate who worked with our group in 2022 and 2023, played a
substantial role in developing the extension. Achyudhan Kutuva developed BNG
Playground. Adam Husar led the development of MCell4, which integrates
particle-based stochastic simulation with rule-based modeling [@Husar2024].
MCell4 was developed as part of my longtime collaboration with Tom Bartol
and Terry Sejnowski at the Salk Institute, and it built on earlier work by
José-Juan Tapia, Ali Sinan Saglam, and Jacob Czech.

At Los Alamos and at Northern Arizona University, Bill Hlavacek, Richard
Posner, and their colleagues have extended BioNetGen with tools for
simulation and parameter estimation. Jin Yang, Michael Monine, Joshua
Colvin, and Ryan Gutenkunst developed network-free simulation methods and
RuleMonkey [@Yang2008; @Colvin2010]; Brandon Thomas, Lily Chylek, and Joshua
Colvin developed BioNetFit [@Thomas2016]; Eshan Mitra and Ryan Suderman
developed PyBioNetFit [@Mitra2019]; and Yen Ting Lin and Song Feng developed
the partial scaling algorithm [@Lin2019]. Bill Hlavacek also wrote bngsim,
which produced every simulation in this book. The commit histories of the
[RuleWorld](https://github.com/RuleWorld) repositories record many further
contributions. Alan Perelson, Walter Fontana, and Michael Hucka did not
contribute directly to BioNetGen, but they encouraged its development in a
variety of ways, some intentional and some not. Vincent Danos independently
envisioned rule-based modeling as a solution to the problem of
combinatorial complexity, and his work inspired, directly and indirectly,
many of the subsequent developments in BioNetGen. He and his
collaborators in developing the Kappa language, including Jean Krivine and
Jérôme Feret, made major contributions to the theory and applications of
rule-based modeling [@Danos2007].

Development of BioNetGen has been supported by the National Institutes of
Health, through the National Center for Multiscale Modeling of Biological
Systems (MMBioS, P41GM103712), which ended in 2022, and grants GM076570,
GM085273, AI35997, and
CA109552; by the National Science Foundation (grant 0829788); by the
Arizona Biomedical Research Commission; and by the Department of
Computational Biology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine.
Work at Los Alamos National Laboratory was performed under Department of
Energy contract DE-AC52-06NA25396.

Finally, I thank the students of all ages and career stages who have taken
the time to learn BioNetGen and to develop models with it. Their enthusiasm
has been the main encouragement for me to assemble this book.
